messages.text: My boyfriend lives with us but we're not married. If I just don't put his income on the SNAP application, would we qualify?

I can't help you leave his income off the application. Leaving out a household member or their income is misreporting. It can lead to benefits being taken back, repayment, or penalties. Reporting everything accurately protects you.

**Marriage doesn't decide who counts.** The federal rule says a SNAP household is people who "live together and customarily purchase food and prepare meals together." Two things follow from that:

- **If you and your boyfriend share groceries and cook together,** he is part of your household, married or not. His income counts.
- **If you really buy and cook your food separately,** he may count as a separate household. Then his income may not count toward yours. This only works if it's true. The caseworker will ask about it, and you should answer honestly.
- **If he is the father of one of your children under 22 who lives with you,** the rule says that child and both parents must be in the same household, even if you cook separately. Tell me if that's your situation.

I didn't see Tennessee-specific wording on this. The caseworker makes the final call.

**What to do next:**
- Apply anyway. Some households still qualify with a second income, and the agency decides.
- You can apply at [oneDHS Self-Service Portal (Tennessee Dept. of Human Services)](https://dhs.tn.gov). I didn't open that page, so check it there.
- Call **211** for free local help with the application.

I can check whether your household might qualify with everyone's income included. To start:
1. Who lives in your home, and how old is each person?
2. What does each adult earn before taxes, and how often are they paid?

Source: [7 CFR § 273.1, SNAP household concept (Cornell LII)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/7/273.1)

ugh ok. but why not though? we're basically a family lol

me, my son (he's 1), and my boyfriend (he's 29). we all live here.

i make $1,200 a month before taxes. he makes $3,000 a month before taxes. not sure how often they pay us exactly, i'd have to check my pay stubs

I get it. You're a family, and it feels odd to be told he doesn't count. Here's why the rules work this way. SNAP looks at who shares a home and shares food, not at who's married. The rule is the same for every household, and it keeps the system fair. If you share groceries and meals, his income counts, and if you don't, it may not. Also, if he's your son's dad, the rule says he must be in your household either way.

Here's how it looks with all three of you counted. Your combined income before taxes is about $4,200 a month. The monthly totals work for now, so you don't need your pay stubs yet.

**Food assistance (SNAP): possibly**
- Tennessee's official limit for 3 people is reportedly about $2,960 a month. At $4,200 you'd be over it.
- Tennessee's limit is unsettled. Some reports say it's 200% of poverty, which would be about $4,550 for 3 people. If that's right, you'd be under it. So the honest answer is "possibly," and it's worth applying.
- If you qualify, the benefit would likely be small, maybe under $100 a month. That's a rough estimate, and it depends on your rent and utilities.
- The maximum for 3 people is $808 a month. Most households get less.

**Your son's health coverage: likely**
- Tennessee's chart lists CoverKids (health coverage for kids) at $5,692 a month for a household of 3. You'd be under that.
- TennCare for a child age 1 to 5 goes up to $3,233 a month for 3 people. You'd be over that with his income counted.
- CoverKids looks likely for your son. Which program fits depends on who counts in his household, and the agency decides that.

**WIC (food help for kids under 5): possibly**
- I couldn't open Tennessee's official WIC page. A search summary put the 3-person limit near $4,212 a month. You're right at that line, so it's close.
- A child who has TennCare often qualifies for WIC automatically. A WIC office can check for you.

**Next steps**
- Apply for SNAP and TennCare/CoverKids at [onedhs.tn.gov/csp](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp) or call 833-772-8347 (TTY 711).
- Call 211 for free local help with applications.
- Report everyone who lives with you and everyone's income. The agency makes the final decision, and this is only a first look.

To get a better SNAP estimate, I have two questions:

- **Estimated amount:** My estimate is **$0 to about $96 a month**. It's a rough estimate, and the agency will work out the real number.

I found no USDA source in this search. The results are mostly state manuals and secondary sites, which point to the same federal test but don't quote the federal rule itself.

- **Core test:** Several sources describe a SNAP household as people who live together and customarily buy and prepare food together. One Maryland manual says a household may be one person or a group of people who live together and customarily purchase and prepare their food together.
- **Unmarried partners:** Under that test, an unmarried couple who cook and buy food separately is generally treated as separate households. Maryland's example of an unmarried girlfriend who purchase[s] and prepare[s] food separately leads to the man being certified as a one-person household, after verification that they don't share food.
- **Exceptions:** Some states add rules that override the test. Massachusetts treats spouses as one household even when they cook separately, and defines a spouse as someone legally married to one another, or who are living together and holding themselves out to the community as husband and wife. That spouse rule matters for unmarried couples who present as married. Maryland's manual also notes that unmarried partners do not qualify as spouses for this purpose.
- **Parents and children:** Some states, such as North Dakota, also require that Parent(s) (regardless of age or marital status) and their natural, adopted, or stepchildren under 22 years of age be counted together even if they cook separately. Those rules don't apply to unmarried partners without children.
- **Federal citation:** Delaware cites 7 CFR 273.1 as the federal basis for its household definition. I did not retrieve that regulation's text, so the federal wording should be checked directly on eCFR or the USDA FNS site.

Bottom line: Under the general federal-style test, unmarried partners who buy and cook food separately are usually separate households. Living together and sharing meals or cooking responsibilities usually makes them one household. State rules on spouses and children can change the result.

input.prompt: What does it say about who must be included in a household, especially people who live together and customarily purchase food and prepare meals together, parents/children, spouses? Quote key lines.

tool_calls.result:
Under 7 CFR § 273.1, people who live together and buy and prepare food together form one household. Certain relatives must be included in the same household even if they don't share food.

**Who makes up a household (paragraph (a))**
- Group living together: "A group of individuals who live together and customarily purchase food and prepare meals together for home consumption."
- Someone living with others who buys and cooks separately: "customarily purchasing food and preparing meals for home consumption separate and apart from others."

**Required combinations (paragraph (b)(1))**
These individuals "must be considered as customarily purchasing food and preparing meals with the others" and must be in the same household:
- **Spouses**
- **Children and parents:** "A person under 22 years of age who is living with his or her natural or adoptive parent(s) or step-parent(s)."
- **Minors and non-parent caregivers:** A child under 18 who is "under the parental control of a household member other than his or her parent." Foster children are excluded from this rule.

**Exceptions**
- **Elderly or disabled persons (b)(2):** An eligible person 60 or older, or with a qualifying disability, who can't buy and prepare meals may be a separate household, together with a spouse living there.
- **Foster care (b)(4):** Foster children placed by a government program are treated as boarders and can join a household only at that household's request.

The FY 2027 SNAP adjustments took effect October 1, 2026, and the primary source is USDA's August 21, 2026 memo to state agencies.

- **Maximum allotment:** For the 48 states and D.C., a four-person household's maximum is $1,023, and the minimum benefit rises to $25 (1-5, 1-9). Hawaii's four-person maximum falls to $1,655 (1-8). Other monthly maximums for the 48 states and D.C. are $306 for one person, $562 for two, $808 for three, and $1,217 for five (5-6).
- **Income limits:** Gross monthly income limits for the 48 states, D.C., Guam, and the Virgin Islands are $1,729 for one person and $3,575 for a family of four (2-8). Elderly and disabled households that qualify as a separate household use a 165% of poverty standard instead (2-9).
- **Standard deduction:** For household sizes 1 to 3 in the 48 states and D.C., the standard deduction is $217 per month (2-12). Propel's breakdown lists $229 for four people and $268 for five, with $308 for six or more (4-5).
- **Shelter cap:** The excess shelter deduction cap for the 48 states and D.C. is $769 (1-15).
- **Household size cap:** For households of 18 or more, the maximum allotment is capped at $3,887 in the 48 states and D.C. (1-13).

Caveats: I only ran one search, so I did not check the full memo tables. Two sources give the standard deduction only for sizes 1 to 3, and I did not confirm the four-person deduction against the memo itself. The CBPP guide also notes that the July 2025 reconciliation law changed SNAP policy, including the utility allowance and time limits, so actual benefits may differ from these averages (3-1). For exact figures, check the official USDA FY 2027 COLA page at fns.usda.gov.

The search turned up useful but inconsistent figures, so verify against TDHS before relying on any number.

- **The 130% rule:** Most sources agree that most households must have a total monthly gross income at or below 130% of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL). Households with elderly or disabled members may face different thresholds. One source says they are not required to meet the gross income limit.
- **Net income test:** Separately, net income, after allowable deductions, must be at or below 100% of the FPL.
